what_the_paper_would_let_us_do: Implement irbesartan from a source with first-order absorption. The only model read in full, Karatza and Karalis 2020 (PMID 32736091, in the archive; two compartments, apparent oral, 32 healthy men, no covariates), absorbs each dose through a delay differential equation, dA0/dt = -ka A0(t - T), with ka T = 0.511 > 1/e, so its input oscillates: 105% of the dose reaches plasma by 6.5 h and 5% flows back to the gut. No nonnegative input the engine can carry gets within 3.5% of that curve (a linear program over any number of pulses), and the best pulse discretisation built (12 default-form oral pulses, as hydrochlorothiazide's Weibull) misses it by 5.8% of the peak (6.4% at a 45 kg woman), ten times the 0.53% standard of docs/adding-a-drug.md, so irbesartan was withheld from PR #818. [decision] for Steven Shafer, raised 2026-11-19: accept Karatza with the 5.8% error stated, or wait for Hedaya and Helmy 2015 (PMID 25545238), whose model the Karatza paper borrowed for its blood-pressure simulations and which is expected to be first order (to be confirmed on the PDF). Karatza's model checked against the Avapro label (not fitted to it): CL/F 13.5 L/h inside the label's 11.8-17.6; Tmax 1.9 h inside 1.5-2 h; terminal half-life 8.2 h against 11-15 h. Karatza's text says nothing is absorbed for the first 1.68 h, but its Table 3 (Tmax 1-2 h at delays to 2.3 h) needs the dose held in the depot before time 0 (Monolix's history convention); that reading reproduces Table 3's Tmax exactly and AUC(0-48) within 0.8%. The Karatza draft (model, test, shared-file patch with the antihypertensive registry record and parameter rows) was not committed; its help-page narrative must be rewritten. Also needed whichever source is used: the drugDefaults row (Antihypertensives), a therapeuticRanges row (none_established), the pregnancy row (not_applicable, ARB fetotoxicity, as valsartan), the antihypertensive registry record and parameters, the three plasma-only rosters, and the Avapro label (archive copy NJ_dailymed-7885b2a8.pdf, md5 12123dca3f7ee8305bd81501a8cc7b64, card papers/digests/NJ_dailymed-7885b2a8.md) in papers/labels with its fdaLabels.csv row.

Liu M, Hu X, Liu J. The effect of hypothermia on isoflurane MAC in children. Anesthesiology 2001;94:429-432. The code says it was read, but its PDF is not in stanpumpRPapers (the archive check in docs/gas-engine-audit/PROMPT.md, section 9), so nobody can re-check the numbers against the source. File the PDF, write its card, and confirm each number below on the PDF. If one differs, change the constant and everything that pins or prints it, in a new pull request. The volatile agents' MAC rests on this paper's regression of isoflurane MAC on temperature in children (37, 34 and 31 C): MAC = 0.0784 T - 1.203. That gives GAS_MAC_ZERO_TEMPERATURE = 1.203/0.0784 = 15.3 C, or 4.6% of the normothermic MAC per degree. The R/physiology.R header says the paper's own text gives 'approximately 5.1%' and a zero at 16.2 C, neither of which follows from its regression. Check all three on the PDF. gasMacTemperatureFactor() applies the regression to sevoflurane, isoflurane and desflurane, to their MAC equivalents, and, since PR #858, to their thresholds (gasThresholdForTemperature()). A copy, PMID_11374601.pdf, is on Dr Shafer's Drive outside the archive, in the folders named CarlisleDownload.

Agerso H, Seiding Larsen L, Riis A, Lovgren U, Karlsson MO, Senderovitz T. Pharmacokinetics and renal excretion of desmopressin after intravenous administration to healthy subjects and renally impaired patients. Br J Clin Pharmacol 2004;58(4):352-358 (PMC1884604). Add intravenous desmopressin (Shafer, 2026-11-25: 0.3 mcg/kg IV to reverse aspirin's platelet dysfunction in the oozing surgical patient). This is the intravenous population model: 24 adults (6 healthy, 18 with renal impairment), 2 mcg IV, plasma and urine fitted together, with creatinine clearance on BOTH the renal clearance (1.74% per 1.67% change in CrCL) and the nonrenal clearance (0.93%); systemic clearance 10 L/h healthy, 2.9 L/h in severe impairment; terminal half-life 3.7 and 10 h. Read the structural model, every parameter and the covariate equations on the PDF; implement R/drugs_desmopressin.R with creatinine = NULL (Cockcroft-Gault through adultEquivalentCreatinine()), anchored at the cohort's demographics, in pg/mL; cross-check clearance against Callreus 1998 (1.77 mL/min/kg) and Ruzicka 2003 (0.35 mL/min/kg in severe renal failure). Davison 1993 (PMID 8447444, in the archive) gives desmopressin's clearance in late pregnancy against postpartum (0.18 against 0.15 L/min) for the pregnancy row. Not in the archive; the PMC PDF sits behind a browser challenge, so save it by hand as PMID_15373927.pdf.

Check the borrowed disposition against the one human measurement there is. R/drugs_carfentanil.R uses sufentanil's disposition on Shafer's judgement, its header saying no human carfentanil kinetics exist and that every human study is PET radiotracer work. Uddayasankar 2018 (Pharmacotherapy 38:e41-e45, doi 10.1002/phar.2117) contradicts that: a recreational exposure with three timed blood samples modelled, an elimination half-life of 5.7 h for carfentanil and 11.8 h for norcarfentanil, and awakening with spontaneous breathing at an interpolated blood concentration of 0.52 ng/mL. Sufentanil's terminal half-life is about 2.5-3.5 h, so that figure points to carfentanil being SLOWER than the congener the model borrows from, the direction the help page already warns about. Read the three sample times and concentrations, the assay, and how the half-life was fitted; then correct the header's and the card's claims either way, and decide (Shafer) whether one case at three samples can move the model's basis or only its documentation. The narrower claim, that no published human population MODEL exists, survives this paper.

what_the_paper_would_let_us_do: Refute the model header's claim that the only in-vivo carfentanil kinetics are in rats, and see whether a second species supports the borrowed disposition's shape. Mutlow 2004 (J Zoo Wildl Med 35:489-96, doi 10.1638/03-074) gives carfentanil pharmacokinetics in eight domestic goats, serial blood to 120 h by LC-MS, rapid absorption and a biphasic decline over 12-48 h. IMPORTANT, and the reason this row was rewritten on 2026-11-25 (CodeRabbit on PR #888): the route is INTRAMUSCULAR only. Every goat had carfentanil 40 ug/kg i.m.; the intravenous, intramuscular and subcutaneous crossover named in the abstract's first sentence is NALTREXONE's, the reversal drug. So this paper gives no intravenous carfentanil arm and no absolute volume or clearance, exactly as Bergh 2019 does not -- the row first claimed the opposite, from reading that sentence and not the rest of the abstract. Read the biphasic parameters and the goats' weights; treat them as evidence about the molecule's shape in a second species, never as a parameter source for people. There is still no intravenous carfentanil study in any species, which is worth stating in the header once read.
